summary: In the present Arabic has no verb “to be”: subject and predicate simply stand side by side, both in the nominative — أَنَا طَالِبٌ “I (am) a student”, الرَّجُلُ مُعَلِّمٌ “the man (is) a teacher”, الْمُعَلِّمُ هُنَا “the teacher (is) here”. This is the nominal sentence. The verb كَانَ “to be” appears in the past (كُنْتُ طَالِبًا, I was a student) and, as يَكُونُ, in the future and in general statements; its predicate goes into the accusative. “Is not” is لَيْسَ, a verb of its own (lesson 8).

head: present — no verb
past — كَانَ + accusative
blocks.caption: After كَانَ the predicate is accusative: -an / -a; a sound feminine plural takes -in (طَالِبَاتٍ). The pronoun is usually dropped, because كَانَ shows the person.

blocks.title: The nominal sentence.
blocks.text: Subject (usually definite or a pronoun) + predicate (usually indefinite), both nominative: الْبِنْتُ طَالِبَةٌ = the girl is a student. The “is” is understood.

blocks.title: Two definite words make a phrase.
blocks.text: الرَّجُلُ الْمُعَلِّمُ = “the man the teacher” (a phrase). For “the man is the teacher” put a pronoun between them: الرَّجُلُ هُوَ الْمُعَلِّمُ.

blocks.title: Place, and “there is”.
blocks.text: الْمُعَلِّمُ هُنَا = the teacher is here. With an indefinite subject the place comes first: هُنَا كِتَابٌ = there is a book here; هُنَاكَ مُشْكِلَةٌ = there is a problem.
Before a plural subject كَانَ stays singular (كَانَ النَّاسُ أَصْدِقَاءَ); after it, it agrees (النَّاسُ كَانُوا أَصْدِقَاءَ) — the word-order rule of Arabic verbs.

askYourself: Is it the present? → no verb: subject + predicate (أَنَا طَالِبٌ).
Is it the past? → كَانَ in the right person (كُنْتُ، كَانَتْ، كَانُوا …) and the predicate in the accusative.
Are subject and predicate both definite? → put هُوَ / هِيَ / هُمْ between them.
Is the subject indefinite (“a book is here”)? → start with the place: هُنَا كِتَابٌ.
Is it negative? → لَيْسَ, not لَا (lesson 8).

traps: *أَنَا أَكُونُ طَالِبٌ for “I am a student” is wrong: the plain present needs no verb.
After كَانَ the predicate changes its ending: هُوَ صَدِيقٌ → كَانَ صَدِيقًا.
A verb before its plural subject stays singular: كَانَ النَّاسُ …, but النَّاسُ كَانُوا ….
لَا does not negate a nominal sentence; that is the job of لَيْسَ.

quiz.why: Past = كَانَ, and its predicate is accusative (-an).
Definite subject + indefinite predicate = a sentence with an understood “is”.
An indefinite subject follows the place; الْكِتَابُ هُنَا = the book is here.
كَانُوا agrees with “they”; the predicate is accusative (a diptote: -a).

seeAlso.note: Hebrew also drops “to be” in the present (אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט); its past הָיָה works like كَانَ, and a pronoun can link two definite words, as in Arabic الرَّجُلُ هُوَ الْمُعَلِّمُ.
Chinese 是 links two nouns (我是学生) but not an adjective (我很好); Arabic links both with no word at all.
German needs the verb every time (ich bin, du bist, er ist) — but like Arabic it uses no article with a profession: Ich bin Lehrer = أَنَا مُعَلِّمٌ.
“Is not” has its own verb, لَيْسَ, which puts the predicate in the accusative like كَانَ.

notes.text: Russian has no present “to be” either: Я студент = أَنَا طَالِبٌ; its past был / была agrees in gender like كَانَ / كَانَتْ. One difference: after كَانَ the predicate is accusative (كَانَ طَالِبًا), where Russian uses the nominative or the instrumental (был студентом).
Turkish has no separate verb either (öğrenciyim); Arabic does not even add an ending: أَنَا طَالِبٌ. For the past Turkish adds -di (öğrenciydim), Arabic uses the verb كَانَ (كُنْتُ طَالِبًا).
Hungarian drops van in the 3rd person (Péter tanár, Peter is a teacher); Arabic drops “to be” in every person: أَنَا طَالِبٌ, where Hungarian needs vagyok.
Greek needs είμαι in every person (είμαι φοιτητής); Arabic says nothing in the present — أَنَا طَالِبٌ — and uses كَانَ only for the past and the future.
Spanish chooses between ser and estar (soy estudiante, estoy aquí); Arabic uses no verb for either in the present: أَنَا طَالِبٌ, أَنَا هُنَا.
English cannot drop am / is / are; Arabic has nothing in their place: الرَّجُلُ مُعَلِّمٌ, “the man (is) a teacher” — and no “a” either, the ending -un says it.
French needs être (je suis étudiant); Arabic needs no verb in the present — but, as in French, a bare profession takes no article: أَنَا طَالِبٌ.
German needs sein in every person (ich bin, du bist, er ist); Arabic leaves it out in the present and uses كَانَ for the past.
Hindi ends the sentence with है / हूँ (मैं छात्र हूँ); Arabic needs no verb in the present: أَنَا طَالِبٌ.
Persian adds the copula as an ending (dānešju-am, I am a student); Arabic adds nothing: أَنَا طَالِبٌ.
Marathi needs आहे (मी विद्यार्थी आहे); Arabic needs no verb in the present.
Hebrew also drops “to be” in the present (אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט) and uses הָיָה for the past like كَانَ; only Arabic puts the predicate into the accusative after it.
Japanese ends the sentence with です / だ (学生です); Arabic has no such word in the present: أَنَا طَالِبٌ.
Korean attaches 이다 to the noun (학생이에요); Arabic has nothing in the present and uses the separate verb كَانَ for the past.
Finnish needs olla (olen opettaja); Arabic leaves “to be” out in the present.
Swahili links with ni (Mimi ni mwalimu); Arabic needs no linking word: أَنَا مُعَلِّمٌ.
Chinese needs 是 between two nouns (我是学生) but not before an adjective; Arabic needs nothing in either case.
Vietnamese needs là between two nouns (tôi là sinh viên) but nothing before an adjective (nhà lớn); Arabic needs nothing in either case.
Inuktitut turns the noun itself into a verb with a suffix meaning “be” and a person ending; Arabic adds nothing at all in the present.
